mappings.note: Defines endangered species. The IUCN species categories have no LO in this frame (the three C-2.1 LOs are about forest administrative classes), so the recall-of-terms competency is cited.

Why recorded forest cover has risen (plantation by agencies rather than natural regeneration) requires reading the forest-survey trend against its cause, so the data-analysis competency. Not LO-1, which is about why conservation matters.
Defines vulnerable species: the next IUCN category after qid:105902, same recall level.
Classifies the Himalayan brown bear as a rare species: applying the category list to a named animal, recall.

Shifting cultivation as the agent of deforestation in the north-eastern tribal belts. LO-2 is the only outcome about land-use practices driving degradation; jhum sits alongside grazing and wood cutting there. Not LO-3, which asks for reasons to conserve rather than agents of loss.
Defines endemic species: species-category recall, as with qid:105902 and qid:105904.
Year the Asian cheetah was declared extinct in India: chronological recall.
Names dolomite mining as the threat to Buxa Tiger Reserve: a single case fact. LO-3 is reserved for items that ask the candidate to sort the general causes of biodiversity loss, as at qid:105915.
What the Himalayan yew is (a medicinal plant now in danger): species recall.
Where the Himalayan yew occurs: locational recall of a named species.
Defines monoculture. Terminology recall; LO-2 is cited where the practice is presented as an agent of degradation rather than named.
Where teak monoculture damaged natural forests: locational recall, the 'where' rather than the 'why' of commercial forestry.
What Chir Pine plantations replaced (Himalayan oak and rhododendron): recall of the displaced vegetation, parallel to qid:105913.

Sorting the true from the false causes of India's biodiversity decline is the summarising task LO-3 sets, since those causes are the reasons conservation is required. Not LO-2, which is confined to grazing and wood cutting.
What does and does not follow directly from environmental destruction: the ecological interdependence LO-1 asks the candidate to examine, read from the damage side.
Why we need to conserve forests and wildlife: LO-1 stated verbatim. Not LO-3, which is specifically about biodiversity conservation under sustainable development.
Year the Indian Wildlife Protection Act came into force: statutory recall, not an argument for conservation.
Distinguishing real from spurious threats to the tiger population is the same sorting of causes as qid:105915, so LO-3.
Reserved and protected forests together form the permanent forest estate, which is the reserved/protected/unclassed distinction LO-6 draws. Not LO-7, which is about which class is largest.

Unclassed forests are concentrated in the north-east and Gujarat precisely because they are held by communities and private bodies rather than the state, which is LO-8's 'who controls each class'. LO-6 would fit an item contrasting the degrees of protection.
Defines sacred groves. Terminology recall; LO-1 is cited where the candidate must examine why such conservation matters, as at qid:105926.
Who started the Chipko movement: case recall of a named movement.
Count of India's tiger reserves: a figure, so recall rather than analysis.
Which reason for the depletion of flora and fauna is invalid: the summarising of causes LO-3 covers, same target as qid:105915 in the textbook's own wording.
Distinguishing community-based conservation strategies from state demarcation requires examining how conservation actually works, LO-1. Not LO-3, since no biodiversity rationale is weighed.

Weighing arguments for and against multi-purpose river projects. This item and the 15 that follow are WATER RESOURCES content misfiled into Forest and Wildlife Resources; no forest LO can be cited, and the data-evaluation competency is the honest level for an item that asks the candidate to judge a project's case.
Which is not a fresh-water source: factual recall from the misfiled water block, below C-2.3's evaluative level.
Falkenmark's water-stress threshold: recall of a defined term and its figure.
Requires separating causes of water scarcity from remedies for it (water harvesting and rooftop systems are listed among the options), so analysis rather than the recall of qid:105928.
River on which the Bhakra Nangal project stands: locational recall.
River on which the Hirakud dam stands: locational recall, parallel to qid:105931.
The main use of Bhakra Nangal's water: recall of the project's purpose, not an evaluation of multi-purpose projects (contrast qid:105927).
Names guls and kuls, the Western Himalayan diversion channels: terminology recall.
Names khadins and johads, fields used as rainfed storage: terminology recall.
Names tankas, the underground rainwater tanks of Rajasthan: terminology recall.
Why western Rajasthan now has plentiful water (the Indira Gandhi canal): case recall.
Where bamboo drip irrigation is practised: locational recall.
The state making rooftop rainwater harvesting compulsory: policy recall of a single named case.
Names the village distinguished for rainwater harvesting: case recall.
Which effect of irrigation is NOT adverse requires weighing consequences, so the analysis competency rather than the plain recall used across the rest of the water block.
Separating movements against multi-purpose projects (Narmada Bachao, Tehri) from those that are not (Navdanya, Chipko): recall of what each movement opposed.
